snippet:
“H5 avian influenza viruses are an emergent threat to seal and sea lion populations already facing numerous conservation pressures,” said first author Elizabeth Ashley, a graduate student researcher pursuing a dual degree in veterinary medicine and epidemiology at UC Davis. “Understanding how this virus spreads in coastal ecosystems is critical for protecting vulnerable marine wildlife.” [...] At the end of 2025, in response to a growing number of H5N1 cases in Bay Area seabirds, the team increased surveying efforts, walking the length of the reserve to document and sample any sick or dead bird or mammal throughout the elephant seal breeding season. [...] When the H5N1 highly pathogenic avian influenza virus was discovered on a poultry farm in Asia in 1996, there was little indication that it would become so widespread and so destructive. Within 30 years, it reached every continental region except Oceania, infecting more than 400 million poultry, tens of thousands of elephant seals and sea lions, about 1,000 people and many other mammals and wild birds.

Pinnipeds, which include seals and sea lions, have been hit unusually hard by the virus.
